title: Bruins' 12-4-1 start leans hard on finishing and goaltending
dek: Boston sits third in the league on points, but the chances say they've been a middle-of-the-pack team getting elite results.
text:
Boston is 12-4-1 with 25 points, third in the league by points. Over a 17-game sample, that's the kind of start that bends a season. The question is how much of it is built on things that repeat. Our numbers say less than the standings suggest.

## A record ahead of the chances

The Bruins have scored 63 goals and allowed 40, a +23 goal difference. Their expected goals (a measure of the quality of shots taken and allowed, which tells you how many goals a team would usually score given the chances it creates) are 54.1 for and 52.6 against, a gap of only +1.5. That's a 50.7% share of the expected goals, 14th in the league. They've been a little better than even in how the games were played, and far better than even in how they ended.

The gap comes from two places. Boston has scored 8.9 more goals than its chances usually produce, and its goaltenders have saved 12.6 goals above expected (how many goals a goalie stopped compared with what an average goalie would have stopped on the same shots). Together that's more than 21 goals of help over 17 games. Both can last a while. Neither is a safe bet to hold at this level.

At five-on-five the picture is a bit kinder: a 52% share of the expected goals. That's a modest edge, and it suggests the underlying game is sound even if it isn't dominant.

## The game-by-game arc

The results are streakier than the chances. Boston opened with a 3-0 win over the Rangers, which the shot quality supported (61% deserved to win, meaning the share of simulated replays of every shot that Boston would win). Then came a stretch of losses that were closer to coin flips: 1-4 to Minnesota (56% deserved) and 1-4 to Ottawa (49%).

The most lopsided mismatch between process and result came on October 8. The Bruins beat Utah 6-1 while generating 2.31 expected goals to Utah's 4.50, a game they deserved to win just 19% of the time. Their 4-1 win in Los Angeles (41% deserved) and 4-2 win in Anaheim (45%) were also games they were outplayed in on chances and won anyway.

The reverse also happened. They lost 1-2 in Carolina on 1.86 expected goals to 4.10 (16% deserved), and fell 2-3 in overtime in Dallas on 2.20 to 4.06 (21%). Those two were fair losses. When Boston has been outplayed, it has mostly been outscored too, which is some evidence the team isn't merely lucky.

Lately the results have been strong. The Bruins have won three straight, outscoring opponents 14-8, but the chances only half back it: 53% of the expected goals, with 14 goals on 9.9 expected. Over their last ten they are 7-2-1. They beat Chicago 5-4 in overtime, Vegas 3-2 in a shootout and Pittsburgh 6-2. As Jon Lane of NHL.com posted after the Chicago game, Morgan Geekie tied it with 10 seconds left in the third period and Elias Lindholm won it 2:32 into overtime.

## Special teams and discipline

The power play is the weak spot. Boston generates 0.55 expected goals per game with the man advantage, 28th in the league. That's low enough that the team's goals aren't coming from the power play, which fits the finishing story: they have scored on the chances they do get, mostly at even strength.

The penalty kill is middle of the road, allowing 0.66 expected goals per game, 15th. Boston takes 4.47 penalties a game and draws 4.00, so it spends more time shorthanded than the opponent does. With a bottom-five power play and an average penalty kill, special teams are costing the Bruins a little rather than earning them anything.

## Goaltending

This is where the record is most dependent. Jeremy Swayman has started 12 games with a .912 save percentage and 7.29 goals saved above expected. Last season he was at 26.52 over the whole year, so this is a good start but not an outlier by his own standards.

The surprise is Michael DiPietro, who has made five starts with a .924 save percentage and 4.77 goals saved above expected, against 0.1 all of last season. Over his last five starts (4-1-0) he's at 4.8 goals saved above expected, with a .924 save percentage against hard shots. That is a very small sample, and a goalie who was at 0.1 last year is more likely to drift back toward average than to keep stopping everything. Daniel Wagner of Pass it to Bulis posted that DiPietro's development "was derailed multiple times with the #Canucks," and that ten seasons after he was drafted, he is "on fire." That's a good story and a good run. It isn't yet a reason to expect it to continue.

## The players driving it

David Pastrnak leads the team with 22 points, including eight goals, in 17 games. He plays 20.42 minutes a night and has 6.38 expected goals of his own, so he's scored 1.62 more than his chances would typically give. That's a small overperformance, nothing alarming. Evolving-Hockey's wins-above-replacement figure (an estimate of how many wins a player adds over a freely available replacement) puts him at 2.7 for 2025-26, the best on the roster.

Lindholm has six goals and 14 points, 1.73 above his expected total, and the team does better with him on the ice, by 2.52 percentage points of expected-goals share. James Hagens has six goals in just 13.34 minutes a night, 2.1 above his chances, and Boston's share is up 2.74 points when he plays. A rookie scoring that way on modest minutes is the sort of finishing that tends to cool.

Geekie and JJ Peterka both have four goals and 13 points, about one goal below their chances. They're creating the looks without the payoff, which is the group most likely to give the scoring a lift if the rest cools. Geekie's expected wins above replacement of 3.5 is the highest on the team, well above his 1.6 actual. Pavel Zacha has five goals and 12 points, but Boston's share is 3.17 points worse with him and with Geekie (3.19 points worse).

The real drivers of play are on the other end of the lineup. Charlie McAvoy, in 11 games, has the team 12 points better in expected-goals share when he's on the ice and plays 24.71 minutes a night. Hampus Lindholm is at +9.66 over 17 games, and Sean Kuraly, in six games, is at +14.07. The defense carries the team's underlying numbers more than the forwards do.

## Will it hold?

Probably not at this pace. A team with a middle-of-the-league share of expected goals and a bottom-five power play doesn't usually stay third in points on finishing and saves alone. Over a full season, a +1.5 expected goal difference points to a team closer to .500-plus than to a contender. Regression for finishing and goaltending is not guaranteed to be sharp, since Swayman has a track record and Pastrnak is a real finisher, but a drop is the likely direction.

There's a counterweight. The five-on-five share of 52% is solid, and the best defensive players are driving results. If McAvoy stays healthy and Geekie and Peterka start converting, some of what Hagens, DiPietro and the finishing are giving now could be replaced by better scoring from others. That's the version of this team that holds up.

## What to watch

Three things. First, DiPietro's workload: if he keeps starting, a cooling will show quickly. Second, the power play, because a 28th-ranked unit has room to improve and is the easiest way to add real value. Third, whether the expected-goal share climbs above 51% at five-on-five or the team's wins keep coming in games it didn't deserve. The record is real, and the standings count the same either way. The numbers just suggest Boston is closer to a good team than a great one.
